items.title: 5.4 Factors affecting the rate of enzyme action

source_refs.note: Topic 5.4, printed pages 131-133: temperature, pH (with the optimum pH table), enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.

blocks.text: Enzymes are very sensitive to the environment in which they work. The activity of an enzyme is affected by any change that alters its chemistry and its three-dimensional shape. The main factors are temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.

The shape of a protein is determined by the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions that hold its polypeptide chains in position, and both are easily disrupted by slight changes in temperature. Every enzyme works at its maximum rate at a specific temperature, its optimum temperature; for human enzymes it is 37 degrees Celsius.

blocks.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against temperature from 10 to 70 degrees Celsius. The curve rises slowly, then steeply, to a peak at about 37 degrees marked by a dotted line, then falls steeply to zero at about 60 degrees. Arrows point to the rising part (Enzyme gains kinetic energy), the peak (Optimum temperature) and the falling part (Enzyme being denatured).
blocks.caption: Figure 5.5: Effect of temperature on enzyme activity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.5).

blocks.text: When the temperature falls below the optimum, the bonds that determine the enzyme's shape become less flexible. They do not permit the induced change in the active site that is necessary for enzyme action, so the reaction rate is slow. When the temperature is raised up to a certain limit, the heat adds to the activation energy and so reactions are accelerated; heat also gives kinetic energy to substrate and enzyme molecules, so they move rapidly, collide more frequently and the reaction rate increases. When the temperature is raised well above the optimum, the heat increases the vibrations of the atoms of the enzyme molecule; when these become too violent, the bonds cannot hold the polypeptide chains in position and the globular structure is lost. This is denaturation of the enzyme, which causes a rapid decrease in the rate of enzyme action and may block it completely.

blocks.title: Thermophilic bacteria
blocks.text: Thermophilic bacteria live in hot springs. Their proteins have stronger bonding between their polypeptide arms and can function at 70 degrees Celsius or higher.

All enzymes work at their maximum rate within a narrow range of pH. A slight increase or decrease in this pH retards enzyme activity or blocks it completely. Every enzyme works best at a specific pH, its optimum pH: pepsin is active in an acidic medium (low pH), trypsin shows its optimum activity in an alkaline medium (high pH), and some enzymes such as papain from green papaya work in both acidic and alkaline media.

In the globular structure of an enzyme the polypeptide chains are held by bonds between oppositely charged amino acids, such as glutamic acid (negative) and lysine (positive). These bonds are sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration. Any change in pH can change the ionisation of the amino acids at the active site, and it may also affect the ionisation of the substrate. An extreme change in pH can break the bonds in the enzyme, resulting in denaturation.

blocks.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against pH from 1 to 10 with three bell-shaped curves, each with a dotted line at its peak: Pepsin peaking at about pH 1.6, Salivary amylase at about pH 4.6, and Pancreatic lipase, a lower curve, at about pH 8.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 5.6 puts the pepsin peak at about pH 2 and the pancreatic lipase peak at about pH 9, against the book's own table of optimum pH (pepsin 1.5-1.6, pancreatic lipase 8.0). The peaks are drawn at 1.6 and 8 above.

Enzymes are very efficient, and a small number of enzyme molecules can catalyse the reactions of a large amount of substrate. The overall rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction depends directly on the amount of enzyme present at a given time, if the substrate concentration is unlimited. When the enzyme concentration increases there are more enzyme molecules and more active sites, so more substrate molecules bind with the new active sites and are transformed into products. If the enzyme concentration goes on increasing but the substrate concentration stays the same, no more substrate molecules can attach to enzymes, so the rate stays constant and does not increase further.

blocks.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against enzyme concentration. The line rises straight from the origin, then bends and runs flat along a dotted level; an arrow at the bend is labelled No more substrate to attach with enzyme.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.7: Effect of enzyme concentration on enzyme activity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.7).

blocks.text: If there are enzyme molecules with vacant active sites, an increase in substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction. If the enzyme concentration is kept constant and the amount of substrate is increased, a point is reached where any further increase in substrate no longer increases the rate. When enzyme molecules are free (at low substrate concentration), new substrate molecules bind with the available active sites and more products form in the given time, so the rate of enzyme action increases. When all the active sites are occupied (at high substrate concentration), extra substrate molecules find no free active sites, so the rate does not increase.

blocks.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against substrate concentration. The line rises straight from the origin, then bends and runs flat along a dotted level; an arrow at the bend is labelled No more active sites for substrate.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.8: Effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.8).
